FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives 
Identify the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury (SCI).
Recognize the most common spinal cord syndromes.
Describe the severity of SCI using the International Standards for Neurological Classification of
Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI).
Recognize the most common complications associated with SCI.
Describe acute and long-term management of SCI in general terms.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy 
Epidemiology
SCI affects the population in a bimodal distribution: younger individuals from severe trauma
and elderly patients from minor trauma.




NOTES

Most injuries occur in the cervical spine, and only 1% of patients have complete recovery by
the time of discharge.
Fifty-four percent of SCIs occur in the cervical spine. The remaining injuries are distributed
equally throughout the thoracic (35%), lumbar (10%), and sacral spine (0.4%).
Neurologically, most patients (45.8%) sustain incomplete tetraplegia, followed by incomplete
paraplegia (21%), complete paraplegia (20%), and complete tetraplegia (17.5%). Only 1% of
patients have complete neurologic recovery at the time of hospital discharge.

Epidemiology
The annual incidence of SCI in the United States is approximately 17,700 new cases per
year or 54 cases per 1 million people. Approximately 288,000 people in the United States
are living with a SCI. This number is expected to rise because of the improved survival
rates associated with emerging therapies. SCI occurs in a bimodal fashion, with the
majority of cases in the young/middle-aged or the elderly. Men are four times more likely
to have a SCI than are women.
Younger individuals typically sustain the injury from substantial trauma. Older
individuals usually have preexisting cervical spinal stenosis caused by congenital
narrowing or spondylosis; these patients often sustain the injury from minor falls and
have no associated spinal instability.
Motor vehicle accidents and falls together are responsible for 69.9% of SCIs, with
gunshot wounds (13.8%) and recreational sports injuries (8.2%) accounting for most of
the remaining SCIs. Of note, around 4.6% of SCIs occur during immobilization and
transport of the injured patient.
Pathophysiology
SCI happens in two phases: (1) initial primary injury followed by (2) secondary injury leading to
further damage to the spinal cord. (Figure 1)

9/4/26, 9:38 AM

Figure 1 Illustration shows the primary and secondary phases of spinal cord injury. The
therapies described are shown at their respective sites of action. G-CSF = granulocyte-colony
stimulating factor. (Reproduced from Haller J, Bice M, Lawrence B: Mediating the secondary
effects of spinal cord injury through optimization of key physiologic parameters. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2016;24[3]:160-171.)

Pathophysiology
The initial primary injury from the initial traumatic event causing mechanical damage to
the neural tissue and vascular structures is generally considered irreversible.
Secondary injury originating from biochemical and cellular events, including the release
of free radicals, an overwhelming response and apoptosis, leading to further damage to
the spinal cord and formation of a glial scar. Current management protocols and
emerging therapies aim to attenuate the secondary injury response.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096

SCI can be classified based on the regions of the cord involved and the resulting
symptomatology.
Anterior Cord Syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome results from direct con­tusion to the anterior cord by bone fragments
or from damage to the anterior spinal artery.
Depending on the extent of cord involvement, only posterior column function (propriocep­tion
and light touch) may be present.
The patient’s ability to respond to pain and light touch signifies that the posterior half of the
cord has some intact function.
Central Cord Syndrome
Central cord syndrome results from trauma to the central gray matter in the spinal cord. This
gray matter contains nerve cell bodies and is surrounded by white matter consisting primar­ily
of ascending and descending myelinated tracts. Central gray matter has a higher met­abolic
requirement and is therefore more sus­ceptible to the effects of trauma and ischemia.
Central cord syndrome often results from a minor injury, such as a fall in an older patient with
cervical spinal canal stenosis and hyper­extension of the cervical spine. It is the most common
of the incomplete SCI patterns.
Most patients with central cord syndrome can walk despite severe paralysis of the upper limb.
However, their gait may be spastic and wide-based.
Brown-Séquard Syndrome
Brown-Séquard syndrome is caused by com­plete hemisection of the spinal cord. The classic
mechanism is a stab wound. True Brown-Séquard syndrome is extremely rare.
Brown-Séquard syndrome results in a greater ipsilateral proprioceptive motor loss and greater
contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (two to three segments below).
Affected patients have an excellent prognosis and usually are able to ambulate.
Posterior Cord Syndrome
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
4/31

Posterior cord syndrome results from trauma to the posterior column, posterior horn, and
posterolateral region of the lateral column.
Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration and touch sensation below the lesion level is
typically observed.
Mixed Syndrome
Mixed syndrome is characterized by diffuse involvement of the entire spinal cord.
Affected patients have a good prognosis for recovery.
As with all incomplete SCI syndromes, early motor recovery is the best prognostic indicator.
Conus Medullaris Syndrome
Conus medullaris syndrome results from the compression of the conus medullaris usually
between T12 and L1.
Depending on the level of the lesion, it may present with a mixed picture of upper and lower
motor neuron symptoms.
With higher lesions of the conus medullaris, sacral segments may occasionally show preserved
reflexes such as bulbocavernosus and anal wink (Figure 2).

Figure 2 Illustration of spinal cord injury (SCI) syndromes. The major descending motor tracts
are in yellow, and the major ascending sensory tracts are in blue (A). The patterns of
sensorimotor loss exhibited in patients with SCI syndromes can be explained by damage to
specific spinal cord tracts with sparing of other tracts. For example, the disproportionate
motor impairment of the upper limbs compared with the lower limbs in patients with central
cord syndrome (B) might be explained by the complete, nonselective injury to the corticospinal
tract (which is thought to transmit impulses related to fine hand and finger movements), but
the preservation of the extrapyramidal tracts (which are thought to control gross leg and
proximal arm movements). In addition, the different levels of sensorimotor, pain, and
temperature loss in patients with Brown-Séquard syndrome (ie, the contralateral pain and
temperature loss are detected several levels below that of the ipsilateral sensorimotor loss)
can be explained by the decussation of the lateral spinothalamic tract over several spinal

segments (C). Anterior cord syndrome (D) results in complete motor paralysis from damage to
the corticospinal tract, loss of pain and temperature sensation secondary to damage of the
spinothalamic tract, but preservation of light-touch sensation and proprioception (as the
dorsal columns are generally preserved by this injury). Posterior cord syndrome (E) results in
the reverse, with loss of light-touch sensation and proprioception but preservation of motor
function, and pain and/or temperature sensation. (Reproduced with permission from Ahuja C,
Wilson J, Nori S, et al: Traumatic spinal cord injury. Nat Rev Dis Primers
2017;3:17018. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrdp.2017.18.)
Associated Conditions Specific to SCI
Spinal Shock
Spinal shock is defined as a transient acute neurologic syndrome of sensorimotor dysfunction.

Spinal Shock
Spinal shock is characterized by flaccid paralysis and anesthesia below the level of injury.
The duration of spinal shock varies; typically, it resolves within 48 hours. Diagnosis of
complete SCI cannot be made until spinal shock has resolved, as evidenced by the return
of the bulbocavernosus reflex. To elicit this reflex, the clinician performs a rectal
examination, feeling for contraction of the anal sphincter while squeezing the glans
penis or clitoris. When spinal shock has resolved, reflex activity returns in the segments
below the level of injury.
Neurogenic Shock

Neurogenic Shock
Neurogenic shock occurs as a result of hypotension caused by vasodilatation secondary
to loss of sympathetic tone. Typical findings include hypotension; bradycardia; wide
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
7/31

pulse pressure; and warm, pink extremities. As many as 20% of patients with cervical
level injuries experience neurogenic shock.
Injury Classification 
Definitions
Tetraplegia—Loss or impairment of motor or sensory function in the cervical segments of the
spinal cord with resulting impairment of function in the arms, trunk, legs, and pelvic organs.
Paraplegia—Loss or impairment of motor or sensory function in the thoracic, lumbar, or sacral
segments of the spinal cord; arm and hand function is intact, but depending on the level of the
cord injured, impairment in the trunk, legs, and pelvic organs may be present.
Complete injury—An injury with no spared motor or sensory function in the lowest sacral
segments.
Incomplete injury—An injury with partial preservation of sensory or motor function below the
neurologic level, including the lowest sacral segments.
Evaluation/Diagnosis 
History 
All patients presenting as a result of trauma are considered to have a cervical spine injury until
proven otherwise.

History
Any individual involved in a traumatic event is assumed to have a cervical spine injury
until proven otherwise. The treatment of potential spinal injury begins at the accident
scene with proper immobilization using a rigid cervical collar to secure the patient’s neck,
followed by transport on a firm spine board with lateral support devices. In sports-
related injuries, the player’s helmet and shoulder pads should be left in place until arrival
at the hospital, where experienced personnel can remove them simultaneously in a
controlled fashion. The initial evaluation of a patient with spinal trauma includes the
primary survey, resuscitation, and the secondary survey. The initial neurologic evaluation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
8/31

assesses only the patient’s level of alertness and mental status. A thorough assessment
of neurologic status and potential spinal injury is performed during the secondary
survey.
Primary Survey and Resuscitation

Primary Survey and Resuscitation
The primary survey consists of the assessment of the airway, breathing, and circulation.
Maintenance of oxygenation and hemodynamic stability are paramount in attenuating
secondary injury to the damaged spinal cord. When securing an airway, manual in-line
immobilization of the head and neck should be maintained whenever immobilization
devices are removed.
Until proven otherwise, all trauma patients should be assumed to have a spinal injury,
especially those with altered mental status or blunt head trauma. Certain histories,
mechanisms of injury, and physical clues are associated with particular types of spinal
injuries. Polytrauma patients should undergo a visual and manual inspection of the back.
Motorcyclists are more likely to sustain thoracic spinal injuries. Thoracolumbar flexion-
distraction injuries should be suspected in the setting of abdominal ecchymoses or
abrasions from seat belts. Patients with ankylosing spondylitis or diffuse idiopathic
skeletal hyperostosis require extra vigilance because they have an increased risk of
fractures and can experience neurologic deterioration secondary to development of
epidural hematoma. Even minor trauma that results in neck or back pain warrants
supplemental CT evaluation in this population. Nondisplaced fractures commonly occur
in this setting and carry a high rate of delayed or missed diagnosis. These fractures are
typically unstable and can lead to SCI if not stabilized appropriately. Patients with
preexisting spinal deformities, which may occur in the hyperostotic spine, should be
maintained in the pre-injury position of the spine (eg, cervical flexion in a patient with
chin-to-chest deformity). Trying to place the patient in a presumed “normal” spinal
position may exacerbate injury. Inadequate initial stabilization can contribute to further
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
9/31

neurologic deterioration in a patient with an acute SCI and can significantly worsen the
eventual outcome.
Secondary Survey
Secondary survey should include a complete neurologic examination based on the ISNCSCI.

Secondary Survey
The secondary survey involves a thorough evaluation of all organ systems, with an
emphasis on a complete neurologic evaluation using the ISNCSCI.
Prolonged immobilization in a polytrauma patient is associated with numerous
complications, including an increased risk of aspiration, respiratory distress, pneumonia,
pressure injuries in the occipital and sacral areas, and possible increase in intracranial
pressure.
Imaging
CT scan is the most sensitive imaging modality and might be complemented with angiography
for evaluation of vertebral artery injuries and MRI for evaluation of soft-tissue injuries. (Figure
3)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
10/31

Figure 3 Sagittal CT scan of a cervical spine shows a C4 flexion teardrop fracture-dislocation with
active cord compression, which may benefit from immediate inline traction to reduce cord
compression. (Reproduced from Oitment C, Thornley P, Jentzsch T, Pahuta M: Damage control
orthopaedics in spinal trauma. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[24]:e1291-e1302.)

Imaging
A CT scan remains the most sensitive modality to evaluate suspected spine injuries
because of its ability to accurately identify injuries at locations that are difficult to
visualize on plain radiographs, such as the craniocervical junction. CT angiography can
also be used to identify possible concomitant vertebral artery injuries.
Even if no apparent osseous injury is present, instability can exist as a result of soft-
tissue injury of the ligaments, facet capsule, and disks. MRI, which is very sensitive for
acute soft-tissue injury, may be utilized in these instances. However, abnormalities are
found incidentally on MRI in 25% to 40% of patients, suggesting that this modality may
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
11/31

be oversensitive. In obtunded patients, MRI has been used as an adjunctive test, but its
use is limited because of the lack of correlation between MRI findings and clinically
significant injury. MRIs are also of use when assessing severity of SCI.
Physical Examination
Emergency department evaluation

Physical Examination
The respiratory pattern of the patient with SCI provides information regarding the level
of the SCI and the need for ventilatory assistance. A SCI above C5 is more likely to
require intubation. Complete tetraplegia is more likely to require intubation than
incomplete tetraplegia or paraplegia.
After the initial survey and resuscitation have been completed, patients are examined
for signs of obvious injuries to the head, torso, and abdomen. A thorough neurologic
assessment should be performed using SCI grading scales, such as American Spinal
Injury Association (ASIA) score, and rectal tone/sensations (in cases of suspected distal
spinal trauma) should be evaluated. Early neurologic findings may be confounded by
spinal shock.
Neurovascular Examination 
The ISNCSCI should be used to evaluate and document SCI (Resource 1).
The change in AIS grade, neurological level of injury (NLI), ASIA motor score (AMS), and ASIA
sensory score (ASS) between successive neurologic examinations should be determined.
The AMS is the sum of strength grades from 0 to 5 for each of the 10 key muscles, tested
bilaterally, that represent neurologic segments C5 through T1 and L2 through S1, for a total
possible AMS of 100 points .
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
12/31


Neurovascular Examination
The ISNCSCI, published by the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA),1 describes
quantitative measurements of sensory and motor function. These standards represent
the most reliable instrument for assessing the connectivity of the spinal cord. The 2019
revision of the ISNCSCI was released at the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA)
Honolulu, HI, meeting in Spring 2019. This revision introduces two new concepts: (1) a
new taxonomy for documentation of non-SCI related impairments such as peripheral
nerve lesions or pain, and definition of classification rules in the presence of such non-
SCI conditions; and (2) a revised definition of the Zone of Partial Preservation, which now
can be used in some cases of incomplete injuries (ASIA Impairment Scale [AIS] grades B,
C, and D) with absent motor function or sensory function in the most caudal sacral
segments.
Treatment/Management 
General Management Strategies
The “time is spine” concept, focusing on timely delivery of specialized care following acute SCI,
should be applied to SCI patients.
Early inclusion of readaptation management, including prevention of contractures,
maintenance of skin integrity, and intermittent catheterization, reduces complications from
SCI.
“Time is spine”2 consists of the following:
Advanced Trauma Life Support, including resuscitation in case of neurogenic shock
Early transfer to a trauma center specialized in SCI care
Admission to the intensive care unit for hemodynamic stabilization including maintenance of
adequate spinal cord perfusion and arterial pressure control. Current guidelines recommend
a mean arterial pressure between 85 and 90 mm Hg for 7 days following the SCI.
Early spinal decompression and stabilization surgery within 24 hours of the injury if no
contraindication to surgery
Prompt transfer to a specialized SCI unit for intensive functional rehabilitation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
13/31


General Management Strategies
Prevention of contractures and maintenance of range of motion should begin
immediately after the injury.
Maintaining skin integrity is crucial to care of the patient with SCI. Only 4 hours of
continuous pressure on the sacrum is sufficient to cause full-thickness skin necrosis.
Repositioning the patient in a side-lying position at 30° every 2 hours is the most
important intervention for preventing pressure injuries. Physical interventions such as a
rotating bed or special mattress allow for simpler nursing care.
Intermittent catheterization during the chronic phase following the SCI is the most
important factor for reducing urologic problems and increasing the life span of patients
with SCI. Patients with SCI and insensate spinal regions may be at risk for Charcot
arthropathy of the spine. This may not be symptomatic and may present with findings of
autonomic dysreflexia.
Nonsurgical Management
The use of methylprednisolone is controversial.

Nonsurgical Management
Current pharmacologic treatment protocols attempt to attenuate the secondary
pathophysiologic events. The current use of high-dose methylprednisolone in the
treatment of SCI is controversial, primarily because of emerging evidence questioning its
safety and efficacy. Methylprednisolone has historically been used for patients with
acute, nonpenetrating SCIs who are admitted for treatment within 8 hours of injury,
according to the National Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study III (NASCIS III) protocol. For
patients presenting within 3 hours of injury, administration of a 30-mg/kg bolus of
methylprednisolone followed by 5.4 mg/kg/hour for 23 hours is an option for treatment.
For patients presenting 3 to 8 hours after injury, administration of a 30-mg/kg bolus of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
14/31

methylprednisolone followed by 5.4 mg/kg/hr for the next 47 hours is an option for
treatment. The proposed mechanisms by which corticosteroids such as
methylprednisolone are thought to prevent neurologic deterioration by limiting the
secondary injury include decreasing the area of ischemia in the cord; reducing TNF-α
expression and NFκB binding activity; decreasing free radical oxidation and thus
stabilizing cell and lysosomal membranes; and checking the influx of calcium into the
injured cells, thus reducing cord edema.
Surgical Management
Initial closed reduction
Surgical management

Surgical Management
In conscious patients, early closed reduction of cervical spine fracture and/or dislocation
is safe and effective in selected cases. Traction should be discontinued if the patient’s
neurologic state worsens or if overdistraction is observed. Whether the deformity has
been successfully reduced or whether closed reduction has failed, the patient is
immobilized until definitive treatment can be provided.
The possible presence of a herniated disk fragment that has migrated into the spinal
canal raises concern that the fragment could cause compression on the spinal cord
during reduction of the deformity. It is generally accepted that closed reduction can be
attempted before performing the MRI in a conscious patient who is able to describe the
presence of worsening neurologic deficit.Early surgery following SCI is typically
performed within 24 hours of the injury. The Surgical Timing in Acute Spinal Cord Injury
Study (STASCIS) recommends spinal cord decompression within 24 hours in patients
with SCI.3 This early decompression has resulted in an increased likelihood of a two-
grade ASIA impairment score improvement. Other studies have also shown the benefits
of early surgery within 24 hours of the SCI in reducing costs, length of stay, and
complications.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
15/31

Surgery is composed of spinal decompression and stabilization (Figure 4). Spinal
decompression is necessary to limit secondary injury from additional spinal cord
ischemia and should be done early to improve clinical outcome. Spine stabilization
allows early mobilization and rehabilitation as well as limits secondary injury to the
spinal cord.
Figure 4 Images of the cervical spine of a 15-year-old girl who was struck by a motor
vehicle. The patient sustained a C4 teardrop fracture with resultant spinal cord injury
(clinically complete C4 American Spinal Injury Association grade A injury). A, Sagittal T2-
weighted MRI shows spinal cord edema and swelling with some ventral spinal cord
compression from the kyphosis and retropulsed bone fragments. B, Lateral radiograph
demonstrates improved alignment and some immediate decompression of the spinal
canal after the use of cervical traction. C, Postoperative lateral radiograph demonstrates
repair of the fracture via C4 corpectomy and fibular allograft reconstruction with the use
of an anterior plate spanning C3 to C5, which was supplemented by posterior lateral
mass rod-and-screw reconstruction. (Reproduced from Gupta R, Bathen ME, Smith JS,
Levi AD, Bhatia NN, Steward O: Advances in the management of spinal cord injury. J Am
Acad Orthop Surg 2010;18[4]:210-222.)
Complications
Mortality
The risk of mortality increases with more severe injuries, higher injury levels (ie, cervical SCIs
are associated with higher mortality than lumbar SCIs), increasing patient age, the presence of
multisystem trauma, and higher energy injury mechanisms4 (Resource 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
16/31


Mortality
SCI patients continue to have mortality rates that exceed those of age-matched controls.
Estimates for acute in-hospital mortality range from 4% to 17%; after hospital discharge,
annual mortality rates remain persistently high, with 3.8% of patients dying in the first
year after injury, 1.6% in the second year, and 1.2% in each year thereafter.5 Despite
modern medical care, patients with traumatic SCI have a significantly reduced life span.
For example, the life expectancy after SCI for an individual 40 years of age is lowered to
23 years after cervical level 5 (C5)–C8 injury, 20 years after C1–C4 injury, and 8.5 years if
the individual is ventilator dependent.5
Respiratory Dysfunction
Respiratory dysfunction is the leading cause of death in patients with cervical SCI.

Respiratory Dysfunction
The neurologic level of injury has a substantial effect on the function of the respiratory
system. Paralysis of abdominal muscles results in an ineffective cough and impaired
clearance of airway secretions. During acute injury, the forced vital capacity of patients
with tetraplegia is markedly reduced, with a predicted forced vital capacity of 30%, which
improves substantially by 5 weeks and continues to improve until 5 months after injury.
Pressure Injuries
Eighty percent of patients with SCI will have a pressure injury at some time during their
lifetime.

Pressure Injuries
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
17/31

Factors that contribute to pressure injuries include (excessive) pressure, shearing,
friction, and maceration. Other factors include poor nutrition, spasticity, contractures,
heterotopic ossification, and substance abuse. Pressure injuries occur over bony
prominences, including the sacrum, ischium, greater trochanter, and heel.
Neurogenic Bladder
The primary goal of urologic management is to maintain renal function, which includes a low
intravesical pressure.

Neurogenic Bladder
After SCI, the bladder is initially areflexic and the patient is best managed with an
indwelling catheter until medically and/or surgically stable. Detrusor-sphincter
dyssynergia develops in patients with true SCI (above the conus and below the pons).
This condition may result in increased bladder pressure and incomplete bladder
emptying, which can lead to vesicoureteral reflux, hydronephrosis, and subsequent renal
failure. The optimal treatment plan maintains a low resting bladder pressure.
Intermittent catheterization is the preferred bladder management technique after an
acute injury. Bladder volumes should be kept lower than 400 mL. To maintain bladder
pressures, patients may require pharmacologic management, including anticholinergic
agents to relax the detrusor, alpha blockers to lower outlet resistance, and intravesical
botulinum toxin injection to relax the smooth muscle.
Chronic indwelling catheters can be used when a patient cannot or will not perform
intermittent catheterization. However, these catheters are associated with bladder
stones, bacterial colonization, and urethral trauma such as urethral erosion, strictures,
and a higher incidence of bladder cancer. Although patients are at a high risk for urinary
tract infection, they more commonly have bacterial colonization. In addition to pyuria,
symptoms of a urinary tract infection include fever and constitutional symptoms.
Epididymitis and orchitis frequently occur in male patients with chronic indwelling
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
18/31

catheters. Other options for those patients may include a suprapubic catheter or a
continent stoma that can be catheterized.
Gastrointestinal System
After SCI, although the autonomic and intrinsic nervous systems of the gut preserve some
intestinal coordination, colonic dysfunction can be life limiting. Fecal incontinence can occur in
as many as 75% of patients.

Gastrointestinal System
Neurogenic bowel dysfunction can affect personal relationships, family life, and available
free time. Scheduled bowel care after the period of spinal shock should include
determination of premorbid patterns of bowel function. Previous elimination habits
should be identified (eg, morning, post meal, evening). Scheduling a bowel program for
after a meal takes advantage of the gastrocolic reflex. A bowel program should be
designed within the first few weeks after SCI and may be modified throughout the
patient’s lifetime. The rehabilitation team will determine whether the patient has reflexic
or areflexic bowel, which in turn will help direct the patient and family in establishing a
bowel program.
Venous Thromboembolism
Patients with traumatic SCI have the highest risk for development of venous
thromboembolism within the first 2 weeks after an injury. The reported incidence of deep vein
thrombosis (DVT) varies widely depending on the screening tool, with rates ranging from 9% to
100%.

Venous Thromboembolism
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
19/31

Level II medical evidence supports beginning mechanical and chemical prophylaxis on
admission after SCI and withholding chemical prophylaxis 1 day before and 1 day after
surgical intervention. In addition, based on level II evidence, low-dose heparin therapy
alone is not recommended as a prophylactic treatment strategy, and early
administration of DVT prophylaxis within 72 hours is recommended.
Vena cava filters are placed when there are contraindications to anticoagulation, major
bleeding complications, and recurrent embolism while the patient is receiving adequate
therapy. Although filters are effective in reducing the incidence of pulmonary embolism,
they increase the subsequent incidence of DVT and have not been shown to increase
overall survival.
Orthostatic Hypotension
Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a decrease in systolic blood pressure of 20 mm Hg or
more or a reduction in diastolic blood pressure of 10 mm Hg or more with a change in body
position from supine to an upright posture.

Orthostatic Hypotension
Immediately after SCI, orthostatic hypotension is more common in patients with
tetraplegia (prevalence as high as 82%) than in those with paraplegia (50%). Orthostatic
hypotension is evident in the acute period after injury and persists in a substantial
number of patients for many years. Standard mobilization during therapy is reported to
induce blood pressure decreases that are consistent with orthostatic hypotension in 74%
of patients with SCI. Symptoms, which include dizziness, blurred vision, and syncope,
occur in 59% of patients with SCI. Possible mechanisms underlying orthostatic
hypotension include changes in sympathetic activity, altered baroreflex function, the lack
of skeletal muscle pumping activity, cardiovascular deconditioning, and altered salt and
water balance. The descending spinal cardiovascular pathways can be disrupted by SCI;
this results in sympathetic hypoactivity and unopposed prevalence of intact vagal
parasympathetic control.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Spinal Cord Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002096
20/31

External counterpressure applied using devices such as abdominal binders or pressure
stockings may decrease capacitance within the lower extremity and abdominal
vasculature beds, which are major areas of blood pooling. Functional electrical
stimulation may be effective during an orthostatic challenge by redistributing blood
volume from the regions of the body that are below the level of the SCI. Midodrine is the
only pharmacologic intervention that has evidence for use in SCI.
Autonomic Dysfunction
Autonomic dysfunction (autonomic dysreflexia) often depends on the level of SCI.

Autonomic Dysfunction
The autonomic nervous system includes sympathetic, parasympathetic, and enteric
components. In upper cervical SCI, the sympathetic nervous system is decentralized and
the spinal cord is no longer under the control of supraspinal structures. The
cardiovascular results can be life-threatening bradycardia, hypotension, orthostasis, and
autonomic dysreflexia. After upper cervical SCI, systemic arterial pressure drops
secondary to a drop in cardiac output and a drop in total peripheral resistance.
Interestingly, over time, patients are able to maintain blood pressure in a sitting position.
Autonomic dysreflexia (also known as autonomic hyperreflexia) manifests as
hypertension, sweating above the level of injury, pounding headache, and initial
bradycardia. This condition is associated with injury at or above the T6 level. Autonomic
dysreflexia occurs only after spinal shock has resolved. In general, symptoms of
autonomic dysreflexia are caused by problems with urinary drainage. Untreated
autonomic dysreflexia can result in death.
Spasticity
Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone.


Spasticity
Spasticity is not always a negative condition because it can be beneficial in enabling
patients to bear weight during transfers and improve bed mobility. However, many
uncontrolled movements can result in complications such as contractures, fracture,
chronic hip dislocation, and pressure sores. In addition to range of motion, other
physical modalities (eg, cold and bracing) can modify spasticity.
Pharmacologic treatment is often required to manage spasticity. Treatments include
gamma-aminobutyric acid modulators and drugs that affect ion flux, such as dantrolene
sodium, monoamine agents, and cannabinoids. Local pharmacologic therapies may
include botulinum toxin injection.
Osteoporosis
After SCI, regional osteoporosis syndrome may develop, with loss of 20% to 50% of bone mass
in the lower extremities within the first few months.

Osteoporosis
Typically, bone resorption begins at approximately week 4 after injury. Peak mobilization
of calcium occurs approximately in the 16th week after injury, but it can continue for as
many as 2 years before a new level of bone density is established.
Osteoporosis is most common in the distal femur and proximal tibia. Interestingly, SCI is
not associated with osteoporosis in the spine. Femoral fractures may occur with minor
trauma associated with transfers or range of motion therapy. Although orthopaedic
consultation is essential, femoral fractures can be managed nonsurgically in many
patients. There is an increased risk of fractures from disuse osteoporosis after SCI.

Heterotopic Ossification
Heterotopic ossification is lamellar bone formation that occurs around a joint, often resulting
in substantial loss of range of motion and sometimes resulting in incomplete ankylosis.

Heterotopic Ossification
Heterotopic ossification typically presents below the neurologic level of injury and is
marked by erythema, swelling, pain, decreased range of motion, and a low-grade fever.
The differential diagnosis includes DVT, cellulitis, and joint sepsis. The most common
sites for heterotopic ossification in patients with SCI are the hips and knees. A triple-
phase bone scan is the best method for early detection and confirmation.
Sexual Dysfunction
The most common self-reported problem in patients with chronic SCI is sexual dysfunction.

Sexual Dysfunction
In general, based on self-reports, men with incomplete injuries and upper motor neuron
injuries have a better prognosis for achieving functional erection than men with
complete injuries and lower motor neuron injuries. In men with complete SCIs,
reflexogenic erections tend to occur. These erections are mediated by a reflex arc
exclusively in the sacral spinal cord. Tactile input passes through the pudendal nerve
that accompanies the motor fibers; the efferent limb consists of preganglionic axons that
travel via the pelvic nerve to the pelvic plexus to the penis, which can then result in an
erection. Men with incomplete injuries may have psychogenic erections. These are
“mentally induced” erections, which are initiated by various afferent stimuli generated or
received by the brain. The brain receives afferent sensory inputs, and descending
pathways from the brain control outflow from the thoracolumbar sympathetic and
sacral parasympathetic plexuses to the penis. Erectile physiology in men with SCI and in
healthy men is the same. Although the dominant autonomic input for tumescence is

Synergistic autonomic pathways compensate for each other between various
neurotransmitters, including noradrenaline, acetylcholine, and nitric oxide.
Pharmacotherapy uses modulators of smooth muscle by increasing erectogenic
modulators and/or inhibiting erectolytic agents. Options to enhance erection include
oral agents, intracavernosal injection, intraurethral suppository, constriction bands, and
vacuum devices. Penile prostheses, which are used in patients with neuropathy or
genitourinary reconstruction, are not used as frequently in men with SCI because of the
higher infection and erosion rates in this population. SCI negatively affects fertility in
men, causing abnormal sperm motility and morphology.
Fertility in women is generally not affected after SCI, although there is an initial acute
delay in the return of ovulation cycles. Ultimately, however, there is no effect on female
fertility from the injury, although this conclusion is not supported by studies comparing
fertility of women with SCI with an uninjured cohort. Sexual dysfunction also exists in
women with SCI, although this sequela has been less studied than in men.
Rehabilitation
Considerations for rehabilitation include patient physiologic deconditioning and muscle
weakness, aerobic metabolism, positioning, and ability to walk.
Muscle weakness and physiologic deconditioning
Prolonged immobilization of the extremities, bed rest, and inactivity result in pronounced
muscle wasting and physiologic deconditioning in a short time.
Disabled patients expend more energy than unaffected individuals when performing
activities of daily living (ADLs).
Aerobic metabolism
During sustained exercise, metabolism is mainly aerobic.
The principal fuels for aerobic metabolism are carbohydrates and fats.
In aerobic oxidation, substrates are oxidized through a series of enzymatic reactions that
result in the production of adenosine triphosphate for muscular contraction.

A physical conditioning program can increase aerobic capacity by improving cardiac output,
increasing hemoglobin levels, enhancing the capacity of cells to extract oxygen from the
blood, and increasing the muscle mass by hypertrophy.
Areas of concern
Patient positioning
Mobility
Performance of ADLs
Enabling bedridden patients to sit can significantly improve their quality of life and greatly
enhance their opportunities to interact with other people.
For some patients, casts or orthotic devices may be required to maintain desired limb
positions.
Aggressive joint motion exercises are necessary to prevent contractures.
Factors influencing a patient’s ability to walk
Limb stability
Motor control
Good balance reactions
Adequate proprioception
Equipment and devices that aid in movement (eg, canes, walkers, wheelchairs)
These aids should always have the least complex design needed to accomplish the goal.
They should be selected based on the patient’s cognitive and physical levels of function.
Developing appropriate exercises and activities
Considerations include joint range of motion, muscle tone, motor control, and cognitive
function of the patient.
Cognitive function considerations
Even confused and agitated patients may respond positively to simple, familiar functional
activities such as face washing and teeth brushing.
Patients with higher cognitive function should be encouraged to perform hygiene,
grooming, dressing, and feeding activities.
Physical therapy prescription
Components include the diagnosis, functional deficits to be addressed, management goals,
and any precautions or restrictions.
The prescription also should specify whether modalities can be used, the need for orthoses,
and the weight-bearing capacity of the arm or leg.
The frequency and duration of the therapy also should be specified.

A home exercise program may be initially appropriate for minor conditions or for motivated,
intelligent patients.
Home exercise has the advantage of convenience but the disadvantage that it lacks
supervision and coaching.
High-level home exercise programs may not be appropriate for patients with balance or
other safety issues.
Generally, a formal physical therapy program is followed up by a maintenance home exercise
program.
Expected Outcomes and Management Based on Level of Injury
Patients’ outcome depends on the level of injury because it influences key muscles in allowing
the patient to breathe independently, move the extremities, and maintain trunk control.6
C1-3–level Function
The key muscles are the sternocleidomastoid muscle, cervical paraspinal muscles, and neck
accessories.
Tracheostomy and long-term ventilatory assistance can be required.
Motorized wheelchair with cephalic control is typically required.
Total assistance for ADLs is usually required.
Most patients require around-the-clock care.
C4-level Function
The key muscles are the diaphragm and the trapezius and neck muscles.
Head control is present.
With a functioning diaphragm, long-term ventilatory support is generally not needed.
Tracheostomy and mechanical ventilatory assistance may be required initially.
Wheelchair mobility is possible using “sip-and-puff” controls.
Newer assistive technology using voice controls for ADLs is becoming available.
Most patients require around-the-clock care.
C5-level Function

Key muscles are the deltoid and biceps, which are used for shoulder abduction and elbow
flexion.
Surgical goals are to provide active elbow and wrist extension and to restore the ability to
pinch the thumb against the index finger.
Transferring the posterior deltoid to the triceps muscle provides active elbow extension.
Transferring the brachioradialis to the extensor carpi radialis brevis provides active wrist
extension.
Attaching the flexor pollicis longus tendon to the distal radius and fusing the interphalangeal
joint of the thumb provides key pinch by tenodesis when the wrist is extended.
Patients with C5-level injuries may use a power wheelchair with hand controls. Some may even
be able to use manual wheelchairs with grip enhancements, although tremendous energy is
required to do so.
These patients may assist with bed mobility and transfers, although they require attendant
care for ADLs and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). Assistive devices are available
for answering phones, using computers, and driving.
C6-level Function
Key muscles are the wrist extensors, which enable the patient to manually propel a wheelchair
and transfer from one position to another. This is the highest level at which a patient
conceivably can live without an attendant.
Surgical goals are to restore lateral pinch and active grasp.
Lateral pinch can be restored by tenodesis of the thumb flexor or transfer of the
brachioradialis to the flexor pollicis longus.
Active grasp can be restored by transfer of the pronator teres to the flexor digitorum
profundus.
These patients may use a manual wheelchair with grip enhancements, although most prefer a
power wheelchair. Bed-to-chair transfers may be performed independently using a sliding
board, although most patients prefer setup assistance. These patients can perform upper
body dressing but need assistance with lower body dressing.
C7-level Function
The key muscle is the triceps.

Patients with intact triceps function should be able to transfer and live independently if no
other complications are present.
Surgical goals are active thumb flexion for pinch, active finger flexion for grasp, and hand
opening by extensor tenodesis.
Transfer of the brachioradialis to the flexor pollicis longus provides active pinch.
Transfer of the pronator teres to the flexor digitorum profundus allows active finger flexion
and grasp.
If the finger extensors are weak, tenodesis of these tendons to the radius provides hand
opening with wrist flexion.
Patients with C7-level function can perform most ADLs and IADLs independently or with
minimal assistance. A manual wheelchair can be used, although uneven surfaces can present
challenges.
C8-level Function
Key muscles are the finger and thumb flexors, which enable a gross grasp.
A functioning flexor pollicis longus enables lateral pinch between the thumb and the side of
the index finger.
Intrinsic muscle function is lacking, and clawing of the fingers usually is present.
Capsulodesis of the metacarpophalangeal joints corrects clawing and improves hand function.
Active intrinsic function can be achieved by splitting the superficial finger flexor tendon of the
ring finger into four slips and transferring these tendons to the lumbrical insertions of each
finger.
Patients with C8-level function and below generally are able to achieve total independence
unless other significant medical comorbidities are present.
T1-9–level Function
Key muscles are the internal and external intercostals, erector spinae, and abdominal muscles.
The upper extremities are fully intact with limited upper trunk stability.
Endurance increased secondary to innervation of intercostals
Lower trunk paralysis and total paralysis of lower extremities
Normal upper extremity function facilitates independent management of bowel and bladder
function.

Key muscles are the intercostals, external obliques, and rectus abdominis.
Good trunk stability is usually maintained.

The patient can use a manual wheelchair for indoor and outdoor activities.
Independent standing can be achieved using forearm crutches or walker and knee-ankle-foot

Key muscles are the abdominals and trunk muscles with varying degrees of lower extremity
